Baby & Child

Taking a child's temperature: choosing and using a thermometer

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A useful temperature reading depends on the device, where you measure and how you use it. The best approach can change as a child grows and becomes able to cooperate. This guide explains the main methods and their limits. If a baby under 3 months has a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, or you suspect fever, seek urgent medical advice; do not delay while trying to obtain a perfect measurement.

Use the number alongside the child's condition

Body temperature varies with the time of day, activity and measurement site. Feeling a warm forehead can prompt a check, but touch cannot tell you the temperature. A digital thermometer gives a more useful record. Tell a clinician both the reading and how it was taken, rather than simply saying that the child felt hot.

A fever often accompanies infection, but its height alone does not show how serious the illness is. A child can be very unwell without a high reading. Ordinary infection-related fever does not automatically cause brain damage; dangerous overheating, such as heatstroke, is a different problem. Pay attention to breathing, alertness, feeding, drinking and other symptoms as well as the display.

Choose for age, ability and local advice

There is no single worldwide age chart for every thermometer. UK NHS advice recommends a digital thermometer in the armpit for children under 5. US pediatric guidance commonly prefers a rectal reading for young infants when an accurate measurement is needed. Ask your child's clinician which approach to use, especially for a premature baby or a child with a medical condition.

An oral reading becomes practical when a child can safely keep the tip under the tongue with their mouth closed, often around age 4–5 or later. Ear thermometers are unsuitable for babies under 6 months, and some guidance or devices set an older minimum age. Forehead devices also have model-specific instructions. Check the permitted age and method rather than assuming all digital thermometers are interchangeable.

Prepare and clean the equipment

Choose a thermometer intended to measure human body temperature and read its instructions before you need it. Check the battery, display units and any required probe cover. Wash your hands and clean the device as directed before and after use. Some contact tips can be washed, while many infrared devices must not be immersed; one cleaning method does not fit every instrument.

Keep a thermometer used in the rectum separate from one used in the mouth, and label them clearly. Do not use an old mercury thermometer because breakage can release toxic mercury and glass. Forehead fever strips measure skin temperature and are not a reliable substitute for an appropriate digital device. Keep equipment out of children's reach between checks.

Taking an armpit reading

Use the digital contact thermometer recommended for this method. Place the tip against dry skin in the centre of the armpit, not against clothing. Bring the child's arm gently against their side so the tip stays covered by skin. Support a young child comfortably and keep the thermometer in place for the time specified by the manufacturer, usually until its completion signal.

Remove it and record the result as an armpit, or axillary, reading. Poor contact or movement can affect the result. Although this is the routine home method in UK guidance, other services use it mainly as an initial check. If the reading seems reassuring but your child looks unwell, seek advice about assessment or another measurement rather than assuming that there is no illness.

Rectal measurement needs particular care

Rectal readings are generally the most accurate, but this is an invasive method. Use it only when appropriate for your child and after a healthcare professional has explained how to do it safely. They should demonstrate positioning, lubrication and the insertion depth for the child's age and the device. Never assume that the same insertion depth is safe for every baby.

Support the child securely and keep hold of the thermometer throughout. Insert gently only to the advised depth, never force it, and stop if there is resistance. Wait for the device's completion signal, then remove, read and clean it. Children with cancer or weakened immunity may need a different method: follow their care team's instructions. If you cannot take a rectal reading, contact the clinician rather than delaying needed care.

Taking an oral reading

Use this method only when the child can cooperate safely. After a hot or cold drink, wait 30 minutes before measuring. Place the tip under one side of the tongue toward the back, following the device instructions. The child should close their lips around it without biting and keep it in position until the thermometer signals that the reading is complete.

Stay with the child during the measurement. If they cannot keep their mouth closed, repeatedly move the tip or are too distressed to manage it, choose another age-appropriate method with professional advice. Do not turn the attempt into a struggle. Record that the measurement was oral, and clean the thermometer according to its instructions.

Taking an ear reading

An ear, or tympanic, thermometer detects infrared heat from inside the ear. A narrow infant ear canal makes this unreliable in babies under 6 months. For an older child whose device and local guidance permit it, use a clean probe and the specified cover. Follow the illustrated instructions for positioning and gently adjusting the outer ear; correct alignment matters.

Do not push the probe farther in to try to obtain a better number. Keep it positioned for the manufacturer's measurement cycle, then record the result as an ear reading. Recent exposure to outdoor cold or heat may affect it, so follow the recommended settling time. An unexpectedly low result should not overrule concerning symptoms or a clinician's request for another method.

Forehead thermometers are not all the same

A digital forehead thermometer may touch and scan across the skin or take a non-contact reading from a specified distance. These are different from disposable fever strips. Some pediatric guidance accepts digital forehead devices across age groups, while other services are more cautious about their use in children. Confirm that the particular model is appropriate and understand what to do with an uncertain result.

For a non-contact device, keep the forehead clean, dry and uncovered. Avoid direct sunlight and nearby heat sources, and let the device adjust to the room as instructed. Hold its sensor at the angle and distance specified for that model while the child stays still. Keep the sensor clean and avoid touching it. Do not substitute a generic distance or scan pattern from another thermometer.

Record the reading without converting it

Write down the number, Celsius or Fahrenheit, the site and the time. Note relevant symptoms and any medicine already given. There is no reliable rule that makes one site equal another by adding or subtracting a degree. Comparing readings taken by the same method is more useful than averaging different devices or reporting a converted estimate.

A rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) is a fever threshold, not a normal upper limit to ignore. Other methods may use different cutoffs, particularly under the arm. If a result seems inconsistent, check positioning and repeat according to the instructions when it is safe to do so. Do not spend time repeating measurements when a young infant may have fever or the child has urgent warning signs.

Keep care focused on comfort and hydration

Offer appropriate fluids and continue usual breastfeeds. Keep clothing and bedding comfortable without overbundling or making the child cold. Cold baths, alcohol rubs and sponging are not a way to treat the cause of fever. Recheck the child's wellbeing regularly rather than trying to make every reading return to a particular number.

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, or ibuprofen may help discomfort when suitable for the child's age and health. Follow the correct product instructions or professional advice; this article does not provide a dosing schedule. Avoid ibuprofen when the child is dehydrated, do not alternate medicines unless a professional advises it, and do not give aspirin unless specifically prescribed. Ask a clinician before treating fever in a young infant, and do not let medicine delay assessment.

Know when measurement should give way to care

A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, or suspected fever, needs urgent medical advice even if they seem well. Seek prompt advice for suspected fever in a baby aged 3–6 months; a reading of 39°C or higher is an urgent warning threshold in NHS guidance. For an older child, worsening symptoms, poor drinking, reduced urine or fever lasting 5 days need assessment, with earlier advice whenever you are worried.

Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, a child who is hard to wake or not responding normally, blue or grey colouring, a non-fading rash, a stiff neck or a first seizure. Suspected heatstroke also needs emergency care. Follow any individual plan for a child with weakened immunity or another serious condition. A low or apparently normal thermometer reading must not delay help for these signs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose a method using the child's age, cooperation, health needs and local clinical guidance.

Use model-specific technique and report the unadjusted reading with its site and units.

Prioritise urgent infant assessment and concerning symptoms over repeated checks or lowering the number.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps explain thermometer choices and prepare a clear record for a clinician. It cannot confirm measurement accuracy, diagnose the cause of fever or replace an individual assessment or medicine plan.

When to seek help

Under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher or suspected fever needs urgent medical advice. Seek emergency help for severe breathing problems, reduced responsiveness, blue or grey colouring, a non-fading rash, stiff neck, first seizure or suspected heatstroke. Do not delay care to repeat a reading or give medicine.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Match the thermometer and method to the child's age, ability and local clinical advice.
  • Follow that device's positioning, cleaning and timing instructions; avoid mercury and fever strips.
  • Record the exact reading, units, site and time without adding or subtracting a degree.
  • Treat the child's symptoms and comfort as important information alongside the number.
  • Young-infant fever and emergency warning signs need care without repeated-measurement delays.

Frequently asked questions

What is a normal rectal temperature for a child?

Temperature varies, but a rectal reading of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher is considered fever. Do not treat 38°C as a reassuring normal upper limit. In a baby under 3 months, that reading or suspected fever needs urgent medical advice.

What should an armpit temperature be?

There is no single number that describes every child's normal reading. Underarm measurements can differ from rectal readings, and services may use different thresholds. Record the value and method without conversion. Seek advice if the child seems unwell even when the number is below 38°C.

How should I take a newborn's temperature in the ear?

Do not rely on an ear thermometer in a baby under 6 months; the ear canal is too narrow for a dependable reading. Ask which method your clinician recommends. For an older child, follow the device's age limit, probe-cover and positioning instructions, without forcing the probe.

Which method is most accurate for a baby?

Rectal measurement is generally most accurate, but it is not the routine recommendation everywhere. UK home guidance uses a digital armpit reading for under-5s, while US guidance often prefers rectal measurement in young infants. Follow local advice and obtain a safe demonstration if rectal measurement is recommended.

Can I add one degree to an armpit reading?

No fixed adjustment reliably converts it to an oral or rectal result. Tell the clinician the original reading and where it was measured. Use the same method for comparisons when appropriate.

Are all forehead thermometers unreliable?

No. Digital forehead devices differ from fever strips, and their performance depends on the model, conditions and technique. Follow its age guidance and instructions. An uncertain reading or an unwell child may need clinical advice or another method.

When can a child use an oral thermometer?

Often around age 4–5 or later, once they can keep it safely under the tongue with closed lips without biting. Follow the device and local advice. Wait 30 minutes after a hot or cold drink, and supervise the measurement.

Must I give medicine whenever the thermometer shows fever?

Not necessarily. Medicine may help discomfort when appropriate, but does not establish the cause or remove the need for assessment. Follow age, weight and product-specific advice. Urgent infant fever or emergency symptoms should not wait for a medicine to work.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
